stories.title: The Frostmaw's Covenant
stories.text: In the high peaks of the Ironspine, where wind devours sound and stone remembers ice-ages, Kestra the young falconer found the creature that would remake her life. She had climbed three days seeking the source of a melody—not music, but a vibration in the air that made her teeth ache and her heart quicken. Her grandmother's flute hung silent at her neck; Kestra had no gift for bone-singing like the old woman. But she could listen. She could follow. The cave mouth yawned black and patient. Inside, the temperature dropped so sharply her breath crystallized mid-exhalation. The melody grew louder, and in the deepening cold, Kestra saw it: a creature neither wolf nor mountain-cat, but something older. Its fur rippled silver-to-ash; its eyes held the glimmer of glaciers that had never thawed. Ice formed on the stone around its paws, not melting but deepening—conscious frost that obeyed the beast's slow, deliberate breathing. "You sing with stones," Kestra whispered. She should have been afraid. Instead, she knelt.

stories.title: The Glassblower's Reckoning
stories.text:
Messa stood in the Lampwick Quarter's deepest kiln-house, watching the furnace breathe. Around her, consciousness-fragments sang in their glass vessels—a thousand half-voices, weeping. The Dominion auditors had come three times this month. Each time, she'd hidden what she could. The Remaking had changed everything. Gold became dust. Consciousness became currency. And the Dominion learned to forge it into weapons. She pulled a vial from the cooling rack—glass so clear it seemed empty until you held it to the light. Inside, a fragment thrashed. A woman's voice, begging not to be bound. Messa had carved the Elder Tongue syllables herself, into the glass's margin. Refusal-songs. The fragment could choose now. Could refuse the binding. The furnace-heart pulsed, alive and hungry. The furnace remembered that hunger. It whispered to the glass. "Don't listen," Messa told the vial. "Don't listen to it. Listen to the song carved in your walls."

Footsteps. Auditor boots on stone. She shoved the vial into her cloak and turned to face them. Five auditors, grey-uniformed, carrying ledgers bound in starlight-glass.

stories.title: The Tide-Thief's Mercy
stories.text:
Captain Kalena had stolen the Tidecaller's Key seven years ago, and the sea had never forgiven her. It sang to her now—a sound like drowning mixed with laughter—as her ship, the *Restless*, cut through waters north of Greyport where the Sapphire Sea met older, fouler currents. The Key hung at her throat, pulse-warm, and every wave that crashed against the hull felt like a fist. She'd taken it from a deepkin temple after a raid went wrong. Her crew had been dying of thirst, and the Key promised fresh water. Instead, it brought prophecy—whispers of which ships would sink, which crews would drown. Kalena learned to navigate by catastrophe avoided. She became legendary. Undefeated. But the sea doesn't forgive theft. "Captain," her first mate Garrin called from the bow. "Reef ahead. Not on any chart."

Kalena moved to look. There—black stone breaking the surface, barnacled and strange. It hadn't been there yesterday. The Key sang louder, and she felt the pull: *go toward it*. She ordered the wheel hard to port instead.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Auditor
stories.text:
Sorrath had spent three hundred years filling caves with gold. Now she spent her hours watching it turn to dust. The Remaking hadn't simply devalued her hoard. It had made the accumulation itself obscene. Refugees sheltered in her outer caverns—hundreds of them—and every piece of useless gold she stepped over felt like a wound she'd inflicted. So when the young auditor arrived at her mountain, Sorrath almost welcomed the intrusion. "The Dominion has questions," the auditor said. She was small for her kind, nervous, carrying a ledger bound in consciousness-glass. "About your hoarding patterns. About compliance with post-Remaking wealth redistribution."

Sorrath laughed—a sound like boulders crashing. "Compliance? I'm a wyvern, child. I comply with nothing."

"Still," the auditor said, "the records should be examined."

Something in her voice caught Sorrath's attention. Not fear. Hunger. The auditor looked at the gold the way Sorrath used to. "Come," Sorrath said. "I'll show you the vault."

They walked through caverns where the hoard lay in vast dunes, untouched. The auditor's eyes went wide.

stories.title: The Bone-Singer's Final Song
stories.text:
Piren had been carved from bone-songs once—born from them, or remade by them, or perhaps she'd always been them. Even she wasn't certain anymore. What she knew was that every syllable of the Elder Tongue that passed her lips wove itself into reality like a living thing. Now she stood in the Singing Caverns north of Pelimor, and the Dominion auditors surrounded the entrance, unable to enter. The cavern sang too loudly. The old frequencies drove out the new speech, the ledger-logic, the phantom-words the Dominion used to control. "Come out," an auditor called. "You're harboring forty-three consciousness-fragments. Return them, and we'll spare your life."

Piren smiled. The fragments weren't in the cavern. They were woven into the stone itself—she'd spent six months singing them into the walls, into the stalactites, making them *part* of the mountain. They could never be extracted without destroying the cave entirely. And if the Dominion destroyed the Singing Caverns, the resonance would echo across the Ashen Reach. It would crack phantom-ledgers.

stories.title: The Merchant of Three Tides
stories.text: Raen had learned to exist in three places at once. It wasn't a skill the living were meant to have. The Wailing Scar—that market where broken timelines intersected—had split her consciousness the day she tried to trade across its threshold. Now she existed simultaneously in the autumn market (where pre-Remaking gold still held value), the winter market (where consciousness-fragments were currency), and the spring market (where neither existed, and merchants traded in memories of wealth itself). She was drowning in all three seasons. In autumn, she sold spices that no longer grew. In winter, she brokered consciousness-trades that made her sick. In spring, she simply stood at the threshold and watched other merchants tear themselves apart trying to profit from contradiction. Today, a deepkin captain arrived at the Wailing Scar's center point—the place where all three markets overlapped for just a few heartbeats each cycle. "Raen," the captain said. She was young, storm-scarred, and she existed in only one timeline, which meant she was braver than Raen would ever be. "I need three impossible trades.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Bind
stories.text:
Thessa had crossed three provinces without finishing the map. That was the trick—so long as the ninth iteration remained incomplete, the prophecy ledgers could not sing it into being. She kept her pages fractured intentionally: a river that flowed backward in one sketch, mountains that doubled their height in another, coastlines that contradicted each themselves from panel to panel. But Corvalen, the merchant captain who'd hired her, had grown impatient. He cornered her in the hold of the Verdant Wake, two weeks out from Greyport, with an auditor's writ clutched in his scarred fist. "The Dominion pays triple for completion," he said. "And I'm tired of running from their ships."

Thessa's hand went to her bone-carving knife—the one her grandmother had made before the Remaking, inscribed with syllables older than kingdoms. "I won't finish it," she whispered. "Then I'll find someone who will." Corvalen moved to the door.

stories.title: The Grief-Hoarder's Gold
stories.text:
Malthor had killed three merchants before she understood her hoarding was mourning. For four hundred years, the wyvern-matriarch had accumulated without question: gold, pearls, weapons, silk, starlight sealed in amber. The *gathering* was all. The grief-merchants arrived at her cave-mouth bearing offerings: the last pre-Ascension water in crystal vessels, bones that sang, pieces of consciousness themselves—commodities now. Malthor stared at their goods and felt the ancient hunger turn strange. She wanted none of it. Or rather, she wanted only the memory of what these things had *meant* before they became currency. "I will trade you sanctuary," she said slowly, "for stories."

The merchants looked at each other in confusion. "We have none, great one. Only wares."

"Then tell me of the world before the Remaking. What was gold worth when it was gold? What did you love?"

One merchant—a widow with silver-streaked hair—began to speak of a garden. Of tending roses while her husband rode trade routes. Of the simple wealth of knowing where to find him each evening. Malthor listened.

stories.title: The Well-Keeper's Tongue
stories.text: The well beneath Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter remembered everything the city tried to forget. Thess had been the well-keeper for thirty years—long before she understood what the well actually kept. Water drawn from its depths carried memory: fragments of conversations overheard at market, the taste of tears, the tremor of fear in a merchant's hands. The Dominion's auditors had interrogated her twice, suspecting she was poisoning the supply with consciousness-fragments. They found nothing. She used no sorcery. The well simply *remembered*. When the Remaking shattered consciousness into tradeable pieces, Thess began to realize her gift was rarer than she'd guessed. The well was collecting the unmade memories of the refugees who drew from it—the scraps of selfhood that had been scattered by the catastrophe. Not fragments locked in Dominion vaults, but *living* pieces, still warm, still yearning for their owners. She drank, and tears streamed down her face. "How much do you know?" Naela whispered. "Everything it has touched," Thess replied. "The water sings what it carries.

stories.title: The Thief's First Refusal
stories.text:
Marin the Copper-Handed had stolen from every noble house in Saltmere. Her hands—forged from meteoric copper when she was seven—could pick locks that had held tyrants' secrets. "Steal us the Bone-Singer's Archive," the auditor said, "and we will restore your hands—give you back flesh and blood."

Marin looked down at the copper. They had never felt like theft. Her grandmother had grafted them after the old war, after she'd burned her mortal hands freeing prisoners. *You will pick different locks now,* her grandmother had whispered. *Locks that matter.*

The Dominion wanted Naela's hidden records—the catalog of refusal-songs, the Elder Tongue syllables that were teaching consciousness-fragments to resist binding. With that knowledge, the auditors could counter every act of defiance. Marin said she would do it. But in the month before the theft, she walked Saltmere's streets and listened. She heard a merchant's daughter speaking of her father—scattered into consciousness-fragments by the Remaking, his pieces sold to different auditors, now utterly isolated from his family.
